borders.before: the lecture opening, course introductions, and the stated learning objectives for the session
borders.after: the core definition of cancer as a genetic and evolutionary disease requiring a permissive microenvironment
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is opening framing and learning outcomes, while subtopic 2 begins the substantive content by defining what cancer is at the cellular and genetic levels.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no reason to move the border because subtopic 1 contains only preliminary framing and subtopic 2 directly starts the core scientific discussion.
borders.caseForRemoving: Opening framing must be kept separate from the first substantive topic of the lecture.

borders.before: epidemiological variations in global cancer incidences and the interplay between genetic predisposition and environmental exposures
borders.after: the role of infectious agents and pathogens such as Helicobacter pylori, HPV, and EBV in driving carcinogenesis
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopics 2–6 establish the high-level concepts of cancer etiology, chance, and epidemiology, whereas subtopic 7 starts examining specific biological and environmental agents, beginning with pathogens.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 6 belongs with the general epidemiological discussion, and subtopic 7 introduces the specific topic of infectious pathogens, making subtopic 7 the exact starting point.
borders.caseForRemoving: General conceptual framing of cancer causation differs markedly from the detailed examination of microbial pathogens and their carcinogenic mechanisms.

borders.before: the detailed historical and mechanistic case study of Burkitt lymphoma driven by EBV and malaria co-infection
borders.after: dietary and chemical mutagens, starting with aflatoxin from Aspergillus and how it forms DNA adducts
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 8 concludes the section on infectious agents, while subtopic 9 shifts focus to chemical mutagens, dietary carcinogens, and physical radiation.
borders.caseForMoving: Burkitt lymphoma in subtopic 8 is explicitly an infectious agent case study, whereas subtopic 9 clearly initiates the discussion of dietary toxins and chemical adducts.
borders.caseForRemoving: Infectious pathogenesis involves unique viral/bacterial mechanisms distinct from direct chemical and physical DNA-damaging mutagens.

borders.before: tissue-specific metabolic activation of carcinogens, focusing on beta-naphthylamine in bladder cancer
borders.after: non-mutagenic carcinogens, tumor promoters, and chronic inflammation, using asbestos-induced mesothelioma as an example
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopics 9–13 focus on direct and indirect mutagens causing DNA adducts and mutations, whereas subtopic 14 introduces non-mutagenic mechanisms and tumor promotion.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 13 is the final mutagen example, and subtopic 14 introduces the new conceptual category of promoters and chronic inflammation.
borders.caseForRemoving: Tumor promotion and non-mutagenic inflammatory microenvironments address a different mechanistic paradigm than direct chemical mutagenesis.

borders.before: a synthesis summarizing how direct mutagens, xenobiotic metabolism, promoters, and host developmental timing contribute to cancer
borders.after: experimental and analytical methods for identifying carcinogens, starting with mutational signatures from genome sequencing
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 summarizes the mechanistic causes of cancer discussed throughout the first half, while subtopic 18 turns to the methodological question of how carcinogenicity is proven.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 17 is clearly a summary of prior mechanisms and should remain in that section; subtopic 18 opens the new question on detection methodologies.
borders.caseForRemoving: The biological mechanisms of carcinogenesis are conceptually distinct from the experimental methodologies used to test and prove carcinogenicity.

borders.before: the Ames test and in vitro bacterial assays for screening mutagens and their metabolic derivatives
borders.after: closing remarks, the balance of risk versus benefit in daily exposures, and the final lecture conclusion
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 21 completes the technical review of experimental assays, while subtopic 22 delivers closing framing, practical takeaways, and the lecture summary.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 21 is strictly about in vitro assay methodology, while subtopic 22 represents the conclusion of the entire lecture.
borders.caseForRemoving: Closing framing should be separated from the preceding technical topic.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2–3 discuss intrinsic and genetic mechanisms of cancer, whereas subtopics 4–6 introduce environmental exposures and epidemiological studies.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2–6 together form a cohesive introductory exploration of cancer etiology, establishing the interplay between bad luck, intrinsic mutations, environmental factors, and population epidemiology.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 7 introduces a survey of oncogenic pathogens, whereas subtopic 8 focuses exclusively on Burkitt lymphoma.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopic 8 serves as the extended in-depth case study illustrating the general viral and microbial principles introduced in subtopic 7.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 9–10 cover dietary toxins and UV radiation, while subtopics 11–13 focus on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and xenobiotic metabolism in cigarette smoke.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: All subtopics from 9 to 13 explore how physical and chemical agents induce DNA damage through adduct formation, thymine dimers, and metabolic bioactivation.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14–15 focus on tumor promotion and inflammation (asbestos, TPA), while subtopics 16–17 focus on host developmental stages and the section summary.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 14–17 collectively cover non-mutagenic, host-specific, and microenvironmental factors (promotion, tissue turnover, developmental timing) that permit malignant outgrowth.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 18 deals with computational mutational signatures from sequencing, whereas subtopics 19–21 deal with classical testing methods (epidemiology, biobanks, animal models, Ames test).
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18–21 together systematically answer the question of how scientists detect, investigate, and prove that an agent causes cancer across genomic, population, in vivo, and in vitro levels.

topics.label: Introduction and Learning Outcomes
topics.groupedBecause: The lecture opens with introductory remarks, lecturer details, course context, and the core learning outcomes for the session.

topics.label: Cancer Etiology: Genetics, Chance, and Environmental Exposure
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics introduce the fundamental framework of cancer as an evolutionary genetic disease influenced by intrinsic mutations, chance, environmental exposures, and epidemiological patterns.

topics.label: Infectious Agents in Carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how viral and bacterial pathogens contribute to cancer, highlighting the epidemiology and molecular mechanism of Burkitt lymphoma.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Chemical and Physical Mutagenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail how physical radiation and chemical carcinogens undergo metabolic activation to induce DNA adducts and specific base mutations.

topics.label: Tumor Promotion, Inflammation, and Host Susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how non-mutagenic promoters, chronic inflammatory microenvironments, and host developmental timing facilitate malignant progression.

topics.label: Methodologies for Determining Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics survey the genomic, epidemiological, in vivo animal, and in vitro experimental approaches used to detect and prove the carcinogenicity of exposures.

topics.label: Conclusion and Risk-Benefit Perspective
topics.groupedBecause: The lecture concludes with a summary of environmental cancer drivers and the risk-versus-benefit trade-offs involved in daily exposures.
